162.title: Bereshit: two creation accounts (Genesis 1–2)
162.hook: chapter one is vast and ordered, chapter two close and earthy; tradition holds both
162.tomorrow: Bereshit: one person, a whole world
162.howItsDone: Jewish readers study Genesis 1 and 2 side by side in the portion of Bereshit, often with midrash on the two names of God and modern commentary on the two accounts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Torah's first letter, bet: closed behind, open ahead. Your line was open ahead. Did you manage an hour of only looking forward? Day one hundred sixty-two.

Think of two photographs of the same person. One is taken from a drone, high above a crowded square: a tiny figure, part of a vast pattern. The other is a close-up: the lines around the eyes, a smudge of flour on one cheek. Which one is true? Both. They just stand in different places. Read the first two chapters of Genesis side by side, and you'll find something like that. The creation of the world is told, and then it's told again, and the two tellings don't sound alike. Today, why the Torah keeps both.
screen: `A DRONE SHOT OF A CROWDED SQUARE.` → `A CLOSE-UP WITH FLOUR ON ONE CHEEK.` → `CREATION, TOLD TWICE.`

segments.voice: Chapter one is the drone shot. It's vast and ordered: light, sky, sea and land, plants, lights in the sky, fish and birds, animals. Six days, each ending, and there was evening and there was morning. God speaks, and it is. Human beings come last, all at once: "male and female created He them," in the image of God. Then chapter two is the close-up. Suddenly we're on the ground. No plants yet, no rain. A mist waters the earth. God, now called by a different name, the LORD God, "formed man of the dust of the ground," and breathes into his nostrils the breath of life. The first human in Hebrew is adam, from adamah, earth. Then a garden, a river, animals brought to be named, and a partner built from his side. Two tellings, two orders, even two names of God. People read this in different ways. Many modern scholars say two older sources were woven together. Traditional Jewish readers hear one Torah showing two sides of the same truth. The midrash notices the two names: one, it says, stands for God's justice and the other for God's mercy, and the world was made with both, because it couldn't stand on either alone. In the twentieth century, Rabbi Joseph Soloveitchik wrote of two Adams: one who builds and masters the world, and one who is lonely and longs for a companion and for God. He said every person is both. So the Torah doesn't choose between the drone and the close-up. It hands you both photographs, and says: this is what a person is.
screen: `CHAPTER ONE: VAST AND ORDERED.` · `CHAPTER TWO: DUST AND BREATH.` · `JUSTICE AND MERCY, TWO NAMES.` · `TWO ADAMS IN EVERY PERSON.` · then, large: `BOTH ARE TRUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold two views of yourself. Settle, and breathe. First, the drone shot: see yourself from high above, one small person in a huge, ordered world, part of something vast. Stay there a few breaths. Then come down close: your breath in your nostrils, your hands, the dust and warmth of you. Stay there too. Don't choose. Let both be true at once. The bell holds the time.
Bereshit. The first portion, where creation is told twice, vast and close, and the tradition keeps both.
Your line: both are true. Today, when you catch yourself arguing one side of something, look for the second photograph. Day one hundred sixty-two.

163.title: Bereshit: one person, a whole world
163.hook: one human was created first, the Mishnah says, to teach that one life is a whole world (Sanhedrin 4:5)
163.tomorrow: Bereshit: you can rule over it
163.howItsDone: Jews often quote Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, that saving one life is like saving a whole world, when teaching about human dignity, medicine and the value of every person.

segments.voice: Yesterday, creation told twice: the drone shot and the close-up. Your line was both are true. Today, the rabbis ask a question about that first human. Day one hundred sixty-three.

A courtroom, nearly two thousand years ago. A life is at stake: the charge carries the death penalty. Before the witnesses speak, the judges take them aside. They don't just say, tell the truth. They give them a short lesson from the book of Genesis. Think about that. Before you speak words that could end a life, a court makes you sit through a Torah lesson. And the lesson is about why God began the human race with just one person. Today's lesson is the one those witnesses heard.
screen: `A COURTROOM, A LIFE AT STAKE.` → `THE JUDGES TAKE THE WITNESSES ASIDE.` → `A LESSON FROM GENESIS FIRST.`

segments.voice: It's in the Mishnah, tractate Sanhedrin. Why was the first human created alone? The Mishnah gives several answers. The first: to teach that whoever destroys a single life, scripture counts it as if they destroyed a whole world. And whoever sustains a single life, as if they sustained a whole world. Adam was one person, and from him came everyone. So every single person carries a whole world inside. Some printed editions add the words, a life of Israel, and many older manuscripts don't have them. Scholars still discuss which reading is earlier, and most people quote the version about any life. Second answer: for the sake of peace. Since everyone comes from one ancestor, no one can say, my father is greater than yours. Third: to show God's greatness. When a person stamps coins from one mold, the Mishnah says, they all come out alike. But God stamped every human from the mold of the first, and not one is like another. And then the Mishnah draws the conclusion, and it's startling. Therefore, each person is obligated to say: for my sake the world was created. Not as arrogance. As responsibility. If the world was made for you, you're answerable for it. And if the world was made for them too, every person you meet is a whole world. That's what the witnesses were meant to feel: you're not testifying about a case. You're holding a world in your hands.
screen: `ONE LIFE IS A WHOLE WORLD.` · `NO ONE CAN SAY MY FATHER IS GREATER.` · `ONE MOLD, AND NO TWO ALIKE.` · `FOR MY SAKE THE WORLD WAS CREATED.` · then, large: `EACH LIFE A WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see one person as a whole world. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you'll see today, maybe someone you usually barely notice: a cashier, a neighbor, a coworker. Picture everything inside them: their childhood, the people they love, what they're afraid of, what they hope for this year. A whole world, as full as yours. Stay with that world for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Bereshit. The first portion, where one human is created first, to teach that each life is a whole world.
Your line: each life a world. Today, treat one person as if their whole world stood in front of you, because it does. Day one hundred sixty-three.

screen: `DAY 163 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BERESHIT: YOU CAN RULE OVER IT.`

164.title: Bereshit: you can rule over it (Genesis 4:7)
164.hook: God tells Cain the urge crouches, but he can master it
164.howItsDone: Jewish ethical teaching speaks of the yetzer hara and the yetzer hatov, the selfish and the good inclinations, and treats study, prayer and habit as ways to steer the urge rather than erase it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mishnah's lesson: one person created first, because each life is a whole world. Your line was each life a world. Whose world did you notice? Day one hundred sixty-four.

You know the moment. Someone says something sharp, and a reply rises in your throat, already loaded. Or the phone is face-down on the table and your hand is already reaching. Or you've had a terrible day and the cabinet with the cookies is right there. There's a pull, and it feels like it's already decided. Cain knew that moment. His offering wasn't accepted and his brother's was, and his face fell, and something hot rose in him. And right then, before anything happened, God spoke to him. Today, what God said, and the word the rabbis built from it.
screen: `A REPLY RISES, ALREADY LOADED.` → `CAIN'S FACE FELL.` → `BEFORE ANYTHING HAPPENED, GOD SPOKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse: "If thou doest well, shall it not be lifted up? and if thou doest not well, sin coucheth at the door; and unto thee is its desire, but thou mayest rule over it." Sin crouches at the door, like an animal waiting. It wants you. But you can rule over it. It's the first time the word sin appears in the Torah, and it arrives with a promise: you're not helpless. The rabbis gave that crouching thing a name: yetzer hara, the evil inclination, or better, the selfish urge. Yetzer comes from a root meaning to form, the same root used when God formed the first human from the dust. The urge is part of how we're made. And here's the surprise: the rabbis don't say it's simply bad. The midrash says that without it, no one would build a house, marry, have children or start a business. That's why, it says, God looked at creation and called it very good, urge and all. The urge is energy. The question is who's steering. The Talmud has God say: I created the evil inclination, and I created Torah as its remedy. And Pirkei Avot asks: who is mighty? The one who conquers their own urge. Not the one who never feels it. Cain, the story goes on, didn't rule it. He went out to the field with his brother. But the verse was spoken before that, and it stayed in the Torah for everyone after him. The urge crouches. It isn't the one in charge. You can rule it.
screen: `SIN CROUCHES AT THE DOOR.` · `YETZER: FROM THE ROOT TO FORM.` · `WITHOUT IT, NO ONE BUILDS A HOUSE.` · `WHO IS MIGHTY? WHO RULES THE URGE.` · then, large: `YOU CAN RULE IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let an urge crouch, and don't obey it. Settle, and breathe. Sit still. Within a minute, some urge will show up: to scratch an itch, shift your weight, check the time, open your eyes. When it comes, don't fight it and don't follow it. Just notice it, crouching at the door. Name it: there's the urge. Breathe once more before you do anything. That breath is ruling it. The bell holds the time.
Yetzer hara. The selfish urge: part of how we're formed, full of energy, crouching at the door, and something a person can rule.
Your line: you can rule it. Today, when an impulse grabs you, delay it by one full minute before you act. Day one hundred sixty-four.

what it means: the selfish urge built into every person, full of energy, and something a person can steer.

165.title: Bereshit: walking with God (Genesis 5:24)
165.hook: among long lists of generations, Enoch "walked with God, and he was not"
165.howItsDone: Jewish readers study the genealogies of Genesis 5 with Rashi and the midrash, and 'walking with God' is often taught as a picture of a steady, everyday religious life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the yetzer hara, the urge that crouches at the door. Your line was you can rule it. Did you delay an impulse by a minute? Today, the last day of the first portion. Day one hundred sixty-five.

Every family has a list like this somewhere. A page in the front of an old Bible, a spreadsheet a cousin made, a chart on a genealogy site. Names, dates, who begat whom. Most of it you skim. Genesis chapter five is that list, from Adam to Noah. Each man is born, has a son, lives so many years, has other sons and daughters. And then, every single time, the same two words: and he died. And he died. And he died. It's like a drumbeat. Until one name, where the drumbeat breaks. Today, the man who didn't get those two words.
screen: `A LIST OF NAMES YOU SKIM.` → `AND HE DIED. AND HE DIED.` → `ONE NAME BREAKS THE DRUMBEAT.`

segments.voice: His name is Enoch, seventh from Adam. And instead of and he died, the Torah says: "And Enoch walked with God, and he was not; for God took him." That's all. One verse, and he's gone. The Torah doesn't explain it, and readers have been wondering ever since. What does it mean, he was not? The rabbis disagree. The midrash records a debate: some teachers read it as praise, others as something more complicated. Rashi says Enoch was righteous, but easily swayed, so God took him early, before he could go wrong. Enoch lived three hundred sixty-five years, far fewer than the others on the list. Other ancient Jewish writings, outside the Hebrew Bible, told great stories of Enoch rising to heaven. The Torah itself says only this. Now look at the verb, walked. In Hebrew it's a special form, vayithalech, meaning walked about, walked around, kept walking. It isn't a single trip. It's a way of life. You go through your days, and God is beside you. The phrase comes back soon, about another man; you'll hear it tomorrow. So that's the first portion, Bereshit, finished. A letter open ahead. Creation told twice. One person, a whole world. An urge you can rule. And, in a long list of names, one man who walked with God. The portion ends on a quiet line: "But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD." A door, open ahead, into the next portion.
screen: `AND HE DIED. AND HE DIED.` · `ENOCH WALKED WITH GOD, AND WAS NOT.` · `THE RABBIS DISAGREE WHY.` · `WALKED: A WAY OF LIFE.` · then, large: `WALK WITH GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk slowly, even sitting still. Settle, and breathe. Imagine walking at an easy pace down a quiet road, one step with each breath in, one step with each breath out. If you pray, you can picture God walking beside you. If you don't, picture whatever you most want beside you on the road: goodness, patience, someone you love. Don't hurry. Just keep walking. The bell holds the time.
Bereshit. The first portion: from the first letter to Enoch, who walked with God, to Noah, who found grace.
Your line: walk with God. Today, take a slow five-minute walk, no phone, and let it be a walk with whatever you hold most holy. Day one hundred sixty-five.

166.title: Noach: whole-hearted (Genesis 6:9)
166.hook: the portion opens by calling Noah tamim, whole
166.howItsDone: Parashat Noach, Genesis 6:9–11:32, is read on the second Shabbat after Simchat Torah; teachers often begin with the debate over 'in his generations' in Rashi and the Talmud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Enoch, who walked with God, and the end of the first portion. Your line was walk with God. Did you take the slow walk? Today, a new portion: Noach. Day one hundred sixty-six.

Think about how you do most things. Eating lunch while answering email. Listening to a friend while half-reading a text. Watching a show while scrolling another screen. We do a lot of things with part of ourselves, and the rest somewhere else. Now think of a moment when you did something with all of you. Holding a newborn. Playing music. A conversation so good you lost track of time. You were whole. The second portion of the Torah opens by describing a man with a single Hebrew word, and it's the word for that. Today's word.
screen: `LUNCH, EMAIL, ANOTHER SCREEN.` → `A MOMENT WITH ALL OF YOU.` → `ONE WORD FOR A WHOLE PERSON.`

segments.voice: The portion is called Noach, Noah, and it begins: "These are the generations of Noah. Noah was in his generations a man righteous and whole-hearted; Noah walked with God." There's yesterday's phrase again: walked with God. And there's today's word. Whole-hearted, in Hebrew, is tamim. It means whole, complete, without a crack. The same word describes an animal fit for an offering: unblemished, nothing missing. Later, God tells Abraham, walk before me and be tamim. And Moses tells the people, "Thou shalt be whole-hearted with the LORD thy God." It's not a word for perfect, as in never making mistakes. It's a word for undivided. All of you, in one place. Then the rabbis notice two small words: in his generations. Why add that? The Talmud records a disagreement. One teacher says it's praise: if Noah was righteous even in a violent generation, imagine what he'd have been in a good one. Another says it's a limit: righteous for his generation; in Abraham's time, he wouldn't have stood out. Rashi quotes both, and doesn't choose. The Torah gives Noah a grand word, and the rabbis ask you to think about it from two sides. What's clear is that Noah was whole in a world that was coming apart. The verses right after say the earth was filled with violence. In the middle of that, one person was undivided. That's what tamim asks. Not perfection. Wholeness, in whatever generation you're in.
screen: `NOAH WAS RIGHTEOUS AND WHOLE-HEARTED.` · `TAMIM: WHOLE, WITHOUT A CRACK.` · `NOT PERFECT. UNDIVIDED.` · `IN HIS GENERATIONS: PRAISE OR LIMIT?` · then, large: `WHOLE-HEARTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be in one place. Settle, and breathe. Notice where the parts of you are: some in this room, some in a worry about tomorrow, some in a conversation from yesterday. Gently call each part back, one at a time, like calling people to the table. Now be here, all of you, for one breath. Then another. If a part wanders off, call it back without scolding. The bell holds the time.
Tamim. Whole, complete, undivided: the word the Torah uses for Noah, and for being whole-hearted with God.
Your line: whole-hearted. Today, do one ordinary thing with all of you: a meal, a conversation, washing a dish, with nothing else open. Day one hundred sixty-six.

167.title: Noach: the window (Genesis 6:16)
167.hook: the ark had a tzohar for light; midrash says it was a glowing stone
167.howItsDone: Jewish readers study the tzohar with Rashi and the midrash, and Hasidic teachers use the double meaning of teivah, ark and word, to teach about entering the words of prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tamim: Noah was whole-hearted, undivided, in a world coming apart. Your line was whole-hearted. What did you do with all of you? Day one hundred sixty-seven.

Imagine the inside of the ark. Not the cheerful picture book version with a giraffe's head poking out the top. The real thing, as the Torah describes it: a huge wooden box, sealed with pitch inside and out, three decks, crowded with animals, and Noah's family. The rain falls for forty days. The door is shut; the text says God shut it. For a year, they're inside. How do you live in a closed box for a year? The blueprint God gives Noah is very short, only a few verses. But one line in it is about light. Today's word is the thing that let it in.
screen: `A HUGE SEALED WOODEN BOX.` → `THE DOOR IS SHUT FOR A YEAR.` → `ONE LINE ABOUT LIGHT.`

segments.voice: God tells Noah to make a tzohar for the ark, and finish it a cubit from the top. What's a tzohar? The word appears only here in the whole Torah, and nobody is completely sure. It seems related to tzohorayim, noon, the brightest part of the day. So it's something to do with light. The rabbis in the midrash offer two answers, and Rashi repeats both. One teacher says it was a window, an opening near the roof. Another says it was a precious stone, a gem that glowed and lit the ark from within. A window lets light in from outside. A glowing stone makes light inside, even when outside is dark. Both are beautiful, and both tell you something. The window says: even in a flood, keep one opening to the world. Don't seal yourself in completely. The stone says: when there's no light outside at all, carry some within. Centuries later, the Hasidic teachers played with a different word in the same verse. The Hebrew for ark, teivah, also means a word. So when God tells Noah to come into the teivah, they heard: come into the word. Step inside the words of your prayer, or your study, and make them a place of shelter, with a light in them. And there's one more thing people notice. The ark was built for storm, not for sailing. It had no rudder, no oars, no sail. Noah couldn't steer. What he could do was make sure there was light inside.
screen: `TZOHAR: FOR LIGHT, ONLY HERE.` · `A WINDOW, OR A GLOWING STONE.` · `TEIVAH: AN ARK, AND A WORD.` · `NO RUDDER, BUT LIGHT INSIDE.` · then, large: `MAKE A WINDOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your window and your stone. Settle, and breathe. Think of something that feels like a flood right now, a worry, a hard stretch. Where's one window: one opening to the world outside it, one person, one place you can look out? Then find a stone: one small light you carry inside, a memory, a word, a reason. Rest your attention on it, and let it glow. The bell holds the time.
Tzohar. The ark's source of light, found only here in the Torah: a window, some say, and some say a glowing stone.
Your line: make a window. Today, open the curtains in a dark room, or reach out to someone who's been shut in. Day one hundred sixty-seven.

168.title: Noach: laws for everyone (Genesis 9:1–7)
168.hook: the rabbis drew seven laws for all humanity from Noah's covenant
168.howItsDone: Jewish law teaches seven Noahide laws as the basic obligations God asks of all humanity, and holds that the righteous of every nation have a share in the world to come.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tzohar: a window, or a glowing stone, light inside the ark. Your line was make a window. Now the flood is over, and the door opens. Day one hundred sixty-eight.

Picture the moment. The ark has landed. The ground is drying. Noah and his family step out onto an empty earth, with the animals scattering into the hills. Everyone alive on the planet is in this one small group. Whatever comes next, every nation, every language, every person who will ever live, starts here. So what does God say to them first? Not a law for one people. A covenant with all of them, and through them with everyone. Today, what the rabbis found in those few verses, and why they called it laws for everyone.
screen: `THE ARK HAS LANDED.` → `EVERYONE ALIVE, IN ONE GROUP.` → `A COVENANT WITH ALL OF THEM.`

segments.voice: God blesses Noah and his sons: be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth. The animals are given as food, but with a limit: don't eat flesh with its life, its blood, still in it. And then the heart of it: "Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed; for in the image of God made He man." Every human life is sacred, because every human carries God's image. A few verses later comes the rainbow, the sign that the flood will never come again. From these verses, and a few others, the rabbis of the Talmud drew seven basic laws for all humanity, called the laws of the children of Noah. Six are things not to do: no idolatry, no cursing God, no murder, no sexual immorality, no theft, and no eating a limb torn from a living animal. And one is something to do: set up courts of justice. Seven laws. Every person on earth, in this view, is a child of Noah, and these are the basic decencies God asks of everyone. What's striking is what this means. Jewish tradition holds that the Torah's six hundred thirteen commandments are for Jews. For everyone else, these seven. And the rabbis taught that the righteous of all nations have a share in the world to come. That's why Judaism has never needed everyone to become Jewish. Of course the seven laws are a Jewish framework, drawn from Jewish reading of the text. But look at most of the list. Don't kill. Don't steal. Don't be cruel to animals. Have courts. That part is a floor that nearly every human society recognizes.
